title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
directAnswer: Build a tree where each node holds up to 26 child links (one per lowercase letter) plus an `isEnd` flag. `insert`, `search`, and `startsWith` all walk character-by-character from the root in O(L) time. The only difference between `search` and `startsWith` is the final check: `search` also requires the landing node's `isEnd` to be true.

remember.pattern: Prefix tree (Trie) with children map + end-of-word flag
remember.formula:
node = root
for ch in word:
    if ch not in node.children: node.children[ch] = TrieNode()
    node = node.children[ch]
node.isEnd = True   # only on insert
# search: walk, return node != null AND node.isEnd
# startsWith: walk, return node != null
rules: Every node needs an **isEnd flag** — without it `search("app")` wrongly succeeds when only `"apple"` was inserted.
`search` and `startsWith` share the same walk; only the **last line differs** (`isEnd` check vs just reaching a node).
On a missing child during a walk, **return false immediately** — don't create the node (that's insert-only behaviour).
Store children as a **map / 26-slot array**, never a list you scan — O(1) child access is the whole point.
The **root is empty** — it represents the empty prefix and owns no character itself.
whenToUse: Many strings sharing common prefixes, and you query by prefix
Autocomplete, spell-check, dictionary, or 'words starting with X'
Need O(L) lookup independent of how many words are stored
A later problem layers wildcard / DFS search on top of a word set
antiSignals: Only need exact membership, no prefix queries → a HashSet is simpler and lighter
Few words, short alphabet, one-off lookup → hashing is fine
Keys aren't strings / sequences → a trie has nothing to branch on
Memory is tight and words share no prefixes → trie wastes node overhead
remember.takeaway: A trie trades memory for prefix superpowers: it makes `startsWith` as cheap as `search`, which a HashSet can never do. Once you can build one from scratch, Add-and-Search-Words (wildcards) and Word Search II (grid + trie) are just DFS layered on this exact skeleton.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can design a data structure from scratch — node shape, pointer plumbing, and the subtle isEnd flag — not just call a library. It's a 'can you build the thing, not use the thing' check.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Forgetting the isEnd flag (so `search` can't tell a full word from a mere prefix), or duplicating the walk logic across all three methods instead of factoring out a single traversal helper.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Factor the shared walk into one private helper, articulate that `search` = `startsWith` + `isEnd`, and note the O(L) cost is independent of the number of stored words — that's the trie's headline advantage over hashing.

problemStatement:
A **trie** (pronounced *try*) or **prefix tree** is a tree data structure used to efficiently store and retrieve keys in a set of strings. There are various applications of this data structure, such as autocomplete and spellchecker.

Implement the `Trie` class:

- `Trie()` initializes the trie object.
- `void insert(String word)` inserts the string `word` into the trie.
- `boolean search(String word)` returns `true` if `word` is in the trie (i.e. was inserted before), and `false` otherwise.
- `boolean startsWith(String prefix)` returns `true` if there is a previously inserted string `word` that has the prefix `prefix`, and `false` otherwise.
constraints: word and prefix consist only of lowercase English letters
At most 3 × 10⁴ calls in total will be made to insert, search, and startsWith
understanding: Design a dictionary that answers two different questions: 'is this EXACT word stored?' (search) and 'is any stored word PREFIXED by this string?' (startsWith). The trie shares the storage of common prefixes so both answers cost O(length-of-query), no matter how many words live inside.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What characters can appear — just lowercase a–z, or full Unicode?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Lowercase English letters only here, so a 26-slot array per node works. For arbitrary characters, switch to a hash map of char → node.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the same word be inserted twice?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, and it's harmless — you'd just re-walk the same path and re-set isEnd to true. If asked to support deletion or counts, store a counter instead of a boolean.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the empty string be inserted or searched?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Constraints say length ≥ 1, but a robust design handles it: inserting "" just sets isEnd on the root, and search("") returns root.isEnd.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is `search` supposed to match prefixes too?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — that's the trap. search needs an EXACT word (isEnd must be true at the landing node); startsWith only needs the path to exist.

The path a→p→p exists, but its last node's isEnd is false — "app" was never inserted as a complete word.
startsWith only needs the path to exist; isEnd is irrelevant. "apple" has the prefix "app".

approaches.name: HashSet of Words (Baseline — fails startsWith)
approaches.whenToMention: Mention briefly to show why the naive 'just store the strings' idea collapses on startsWith — then pivot to the trie.

complexity.time: insert O(L), search O(L), startsWith O(N·L)

hints: If you only had to support insert and exact search, what's the simplest structure? A hash set of the whole words.
Now try to answer startsWith with that set. There's no key for a prefix — you'd have to look at every stored word.
That last realization is the whole reason tries exist: they index by prefix, not by whole word.
approaches.complexityReasoning: insert/search hash a length-L string in O(L). But startsWith has no prefix key, so it must scan all N stored words and test each → O(N·L) per call.
approaches.explanation:
The most literal reading of 'store words, then look them up' is a `HashSet<String>`. `insert` adds the word, `search` is a single `contains` call — both clean and O(L) to hash the string.

**Why it looks good at first.** Two of the three methods are trivial one-liners, and hashing gives average O(1) membership. If the problem stopped at insert + search, this would be the right answer and a trie would be over-engineering.

**Why startsWith breaks it.** A hash set keys on the *whole* word. There is no entry for the prefix `"app"`, so to answer `startsWith("app")` you must iterate every stored word and test `word.startsWith(prefix)`. That's O(N·L) per call — and with up to 3×10⁴ calls, it degrades to quadratic-ish behaviour. The set simply has no notion of 'words sharing a beginning'.

**Why we don't ship this.** The problem deliberately asks for `startsWith` to force a prefix-indexed structure. State this baseline to show you understand the trade, then reach for the trie that makes all three operations O(L).
approaches.insight: A HashSet indexes by the entire key, so it can answer 'is this exact thing present?' but never 'does anything start with this?'. The moment a prefix query appears, you need a structure that *shares and indexes prefixes* — that's the trie.

Using `words.contains(prefix)` for startsWith — that checks exact membership of the prefix, not whether any word begins with it.

approaches.name: Trie with Children Map + isEnd Flag (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'a tree of characters where each node branches per letter and marks whether a word ends here'.

complexity.time: insert O(L), search O(L), startsWith O(L)

hints: What if words that share a prefix shared the same path through a tree, so "app" and "apple" reuse the a→p→p chain?
Give each node a map from next-character to child node, and a boolean isEnd that says 'a complete word stops here'.
insert walks/creates the path and sets isEnd at the last node. search walks and checks isEnd. startsWith walks and just checks the path existed.
approaches.complexityReasoning: All three operations walk exactly one character of the query at a time, doing O(1) child lookup per step, so each is O(L) where L is the query length — completely independent of N, the number of stored words. Space is the sum of all distinct character-edges, bounded by total characters inserted.
approaches.explanation:
Model the dictionary as a tree. The root represents the empty prefix and owns no character. Each node holds a map (or 26-slot array) from a character to its child node, plus an `isEnd` boolean. A word is the path from the root spelling it out, with `isEnd = true` on the final node.

**Why a tree of characters beats a set of words.** Words that share a prefix share a path. `"app"` and `"apple"` both travel a→p→p; only after that do they diverge. This is exactly what makes `startsWith` cheap: to ask 'does any word start with app?' you just walk a→p→p and check the path exists — O(L), no scanning of other words. The set couldn't do this because it had no shared-prefix structure to walk.

**Why the isEnd flag is non-negotiable.** Walking the path tells you the *characters* exist, but not whether a *word* ended there. After inserting only `"apple"`, the path a→p→p exists, so without a flag you couldn't distinguish `search("app")` (should be false) from `search("apple")` (should be true). `isEnd` is the one bit that separates 'a word ends here' from 'this is merely a prefix of some word'. This single flag is the entire difference between `search` and `startsWith`.

**Why all three methods share one walk.** insert, search, and startsWith each step through the query character by character from the root. insert *creates* a missing child; search and startsWith *fail* on a missing child. search additionally checks `isEnd` at the end; startsWith does not. Factoring the walk into one private helper that returns the landing node (or null) keeps the code DRY and makes the `search = walk + isEnd`, `startsWith = walk != null` symmetry obvious.
approaches.insight: A trie is just 'a tree whose edges are characters'. Every string operation becomes a root-to-node walk. The headline win is that cost depends only on the query length L, never on how many words N you've stored — so a dictionary of a million words answers startsWith just as fast as a dictionary of ten. That O(L)-regardless-of-N property is why autocomplete and Word Search II are built on tries.

pitfalls: Omitting isEnd — then search can't distinguish a stored word from a mere prefix (search("app") wrongly returns true).
Creating nodes during search/startsWith — only insert may mutate the tree; the read walk must return null on a missing child.
Duplicating the traversal in all three methods instead of one walk helper — more code, more places to introduce a bug.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the isEnd flag, so search("app") succeeds when only "apple" was inserted.
Using startsWith logic (just reaching a node) inside search — search must also verify isEnd.
Creating child nodes during a read operation (search/startsWith) instead of returning false on a missing edge.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: search without the isEnd check
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If search only verifies that the path exists, it behaves like startsWith — returning true for any prefix of a stored word. search("app") would wrongly return true after only "apple" was inserted.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Mutating the trie during a read
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Copy-pasting insert's 'create child if missing' into the walk silently inserts the query as a side effect, so a later search/startsWith for it returns true even though it was never inserted.

followupVariations.hint: Same trie, but search supports '.' wildcards — DFS that branches over all children on a dot.

followupVariations.title: Word Search II
followupVariations.hint: Build a trie of the word list, then DFS the grid once, pruning branches that fall off the trie.

followupVariations.title: Replace Words
followupVariations.hint: Insert dictionary roots into a trie, then for each word walk until the first isEnd to find the shortest root.

followupVariations.title: Longest Common Prefix
followupVariations.hint: Can be solved with a trie: insert all strings, then walk down while each node has exactly one child and isn't a word end.

patternNote: Canonical Trie (Prefix Tree) design. Recognise it whenever many strings share prefixes and you query by prefix. The children-map + isEnd skeleton is the foundation for Add-and-Search-Words (wildcards) and Word Search II (trie-pruned grid DFS).
